narrative:
The model determined that you have a 94.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is so high, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Both rankings placed you at the very bottom of your cohort (decile 1), far below the average student who is admitted (around the 6th decile). These two early signals of academic performance outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor. At 3.00 it was slightly below the 3.23 average of admitted students, but this actually worked mildly in your favor by nudging the prediction a little closer to passing. Unfortunately, it was not enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 29 was also well below the typical admitted student’s 37, and your middle family income is fairly common among applicants, but neither of these played as large a role as your school performance.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly, and explore schools with different admission thresholds or post-baccalaureate programs that can demonstrate sustained improvement.
